title: Welcomed home (217–220)
hook: as kin welcome a traveler home, good deeds welcome the one who did good

segments.voice: Yesterday, piya: from what is dear comes grief, and Visākhā in wet clothes. Your line was love fully, hold loosely.

At the arrivals gate of an airport, the doors slide open, and someone walks out after a long time away: a soldier, a student back from a year abroad, a grandmother who flew halfway around the world. A little crowd is waiting. Balloons, a handmade sign, a kid who breaks loose and runs. Nobody at that gate is thinking about the traveler's résumé. They're just glad. Today's verse takes that gate and puts it somewhere unexpected.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS GATE.` → `A SIGN, BALLOONS, A KID WHO RUNS.` → `THE GATE, SOMEWHERE UNEXPECTED.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen spends its first verses on the grief that comes from what is dear. It ends with what is dear in a good way. Verse two seventeen, in Max Müller's words, describes a person the world holds dear: one with virtue and insight, who is just, speaks the truth, and "does what is his own business". Then the two verses today is named for. Verse two nineteen: "Kinsmen, friends, and lovers salute a man who has been long away, and returns safe from afar." And verse two twenty: "In like manner his good works receive him who has done good, and has gone from this world to the other;--as kinsmen receive a friend on his return." The Pali word for those good works is puñña, often translated merit: goodness that builds up, like savings. In Buddhist teaching, a person continues after death according to their actions, and here the actions themselves are pictured as family at the gate. The old commentary gives it a story. A generous man named Nandiya built a hall for the monks. The great disciple Moggallāna, the story says, visited a heaven realm and saw a mansion already being prepared there for Nandiya, before Nandiya had even died. Even without picturing heaven, the image is easy to hold: in this verse, a kind deed is sent on ahead, and when the doer arrives, it's waiting at the gate like family with a handmade sign.
screen: `WHAT IS DEAR, IN A GOOD WAY.` · `KIN AT THE GATE.` · `PUÑÑA — GOODNESS THAT BUILDS UP.` · `NANDIYA'S MANSION, AHEAD OF HIM.` · then, large: `GOOD DEEDS GREET YOU.`

segments.voice: Imagine yourself a year from now, coming home after a long day. What small good thing would that future you be glad to find waiting: a drawer cleared, a letter written, a friendship tended, a debt paid, money set aside for someone who needs it? Pick one, picture future you finding it and feeling welcomed, then let the picture go and rest in the breath.
Welcomed home. Verse two twenty: as kin welcome a traveler returning, good deeds welcome the one who did good.
Your line: good deeds greet you. In this verse, they wait at the gate like kin. Two hundred days, well walked.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists make merit through giving, keeping precepts and practice, and often dedicate that merit to others; these verses are commonly cited to describe good deeds as what goes with a person beyond this life.

original.note: Pali: merit, goodness, the good that builds up — in verse 220, puññāni welcome the doer home.

trapdoor: what you thought: be good and you'll be rewarded.
what it means: good deeds go on ahead of you, like family waiting at the arrivals gate.
what a scholar hears: verse 220's puññāni paṭigaṇhanti pictures merit receiving the doer as kin receive a dear one; the commentary ties it to Nandiya.
